title: Incidence and Outcomes of Human Adenovirus Infection and Disease in a Multicenter Cohort of Pediatric Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplant Recipients.

analysis.scope_and_question: The review examines human adenovirus (HAdV) infection and disease in pediatric allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (allo-HCT) recipients, focusing on incidence, progression from infection to disease, and associated mortality within an 180-day post-transplant surveillance period.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: The study is a multicenter cohort analysis conducted at 10 pediatric institutions, following 819 allo-HCT recipients for 180 days post-transplant. Surveillance included blood and stool specimens collected 0–7 days prior to allo-HCT for serum HAdV immunoglobulin G and stool HAdV PCR testing, with outcomes centrally reviewed by a committee using a priori definitions.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: HAdV infection and DNAemia incidence among surveilled patients were 27.1% and 16.0%, respectively. The incidence of proven or probable HAdV disease was 10.9% for the entire cohort and 12.6% among those under surveillance. The attributable case-fatality rate for proven or probable disease was 13.5%. Pretransplant HAdV immunoglobulin G and stool PCR positivity identified a high-risk subgroup with 52.0% infection incidence.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: The review highlights limited data defining HAdV infection, disease, and case-fatality rates in the era of HAdV PCR surveillance testing, indicating a need for standardized surveillance and outcome definitions across institutions.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: Pretransplant serology and stool PCR testing could identify high-risk patients for targeted clinical trials assessing novel HAdV interventions in pediatric allo-HCT recipients, addressing the substantial HAdV-attributable mortality observed.

analysis.summary_en: This review evaluates human adenovirus (HAdV) infection and disease in pediatric allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant (allo-HCT) recipients within a 180-day post-transplant surveillance framework. Among 819 recipients, HAdV infection and DNAemia occurred in 27.1% and 16.0% of surveilled patients, respectively, with proven or probable HAdV disease affecting 10.9% of the cohort and 12.6% of those under surveillance. The attributable case-fatality rate for proven or probable disease was 13.5%. Pretransplant HAdV immunoglobulin G and stool PCR positivity identified a high-risk subgroup with a 52.0% infection incidence. The study underscores the substantial burden of HAdV disease and mortality in this population, emphasizing the need for standardized surveillance and targeted clinical trials to evaluate novel interventions.

title: An inactivated human adenovirus type 55 vaccine attenuates pulmonary pathology in a non-human primate challenge model.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human adenovirus type 55 (HAdV-55) is an emerging respiratory pathogen associated with severe pneumonia and acute respiratory disease, yet no licensed vaccine is currently available.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Here, we evaluated the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of an inactivated HAdV-55 vaccine formulated with aluminum hydroxide (iHAdV-55 + AH) in cynomolgus macaques.
analysis.methods: Animals received a prime-boost intramuscular immunization, and HAdV-55-specific binding IgG and neutralizing antibody responses were monitored longitudinally for up to 52 weeks.
analysis.main_results: Following the high-dose challenge, vaccinated macaques showed reduced pulmonary lesion burden on chest computed tomography, lower relative lung weights, and attenuated histopathological changes compared with PBS controls. In the low-dose challenge model, where overall disease manifestations were milder, vaccinated animals consistently exhibited fewer radiologic abnormalities, reduced inflammatory cell infiltration, and decreased viral shedding in nasal swabs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: Vaccination induced HAdV-55-specific binding and neutralizing antibody responses that remained detectable throughout the 52-week study period.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Together, these findings indicate that iHAdV-55 + AH is immunogenic and attenuates HAdV-55-induced pulmonary pathology in this non-human primate model, supporting further development of inactivated vaccine strategies against severe HAdV-55 infection.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: No evidence of vaccine-enhanced respiratory disease was observed in either challenge setting.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the immunogenicity and protective efficacy of an inactivated HAdV-55 vaccine in cynomolgus macaques. The vaccine was formulated with aluminum hydroxide and administered via a prime-boost intramuscular regimen. The research aimed to address the lack of licensed vaccines for HAdV-55, an emerging respiratory pathogen linked to severe pneumonia and acute respiratory disease. The study involved two challenge models with high and low doses of HAdV-55, and the results showed that vaccinated animals had reduced pulmonary lesion burden, lower lung weights, and attenuated histopathological changes compared to controls. Additionally, vaccinated animals exhibited fewer radiologic abnormalities, reduced inflammation, and decreased viral shedding in nasal swabs. The findings suggest that the vaccine is immunogenic and effective in reducing HAdV-55-induced pulmonary pathology, supporting its development as a strategy against severe infections. However, the study was limited to non-human primates, and no evidence of vaccine-enhanced disease was observed.

title: Lateral Flow Immunochromatographic Assay for Detection of Antibodies Against a Recombinant Human Adenovirus Type 3 Hexon Fragment Using Gold Nanoparticles and Quantum Dots

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human adenoviruses (HAdVs) are widely used as vectors for vaccines and gene therapy; however, pre-existing immunity can reduce their efficacy. Therefore, rapid and accessible serological methods are required to assess antibody levels against adenoviruses.
analysis.study_design_and_population: In this study, we aimed to develop and evaluate LFIA systems based on gold nanoparticles (GNPs) and quantum dots (QDs) using a recombinant HAdV hexon protein. A recombinant HAdV hexon protein fragment (rhHAdV, 35 kDa; amino acids A120-R316) was expressed in Escherichia coli and purified using Ni2+ affinity chromatography.
analysis.methods: Protein identity was confirmed using sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, Western blotting, and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry analyses. Two LFIA formats were developed using Protein G-conjugated GNPs (GNP-G) and QDs (QD-G). Agreement with the reference ELISA was evaluated using 90 human serum samples.
analysis.main_results: The rhHAdV antigen demonstrated reactivity with anti-adenovirus-positive human sera in ELISA. Antibody detection was achieved at serum dilutions of up to 1:300 and 1:1000 for the GNP- and QD-based LFIA, respectively. The GNP-G and QD-G LFIA formats demonstrated positive percent agreements of 96.9% and 100%, respectively, while both assays showed a negative percent agreement of 98.2% compared with the reference ELISA.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings demonstrate the feasibility of a QD-based LFIA for qualitative detection of antibodies reactive with the recombinant HAdV-B3 hexon fragment.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results suggest that QD-based LFIA could be a valuable tool for rapid and accessible serological testing of antibodies against adenoviruses, which is important for monitoring immunity and vaccine efficacy.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study evaluated agreement with the reference ELISA using 90 human serum samples, which may limit generalisability. The evidence strength is moderate due to the limited sample size and the absence of long-term follow-up data.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to develop and evaluate lateral flow immunochromatographic assays (LFIA) for detecting antibodies against a recombinant human adenovirus type 3 hexon fragment using gold nanoparticles (GNPs) and quantum dots (QDs). The researchers expressed and purified the recombinant hexon protein fragment (rhHAdV) in Escherichia coli and confirmed its identity through sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, Western blotting, and liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Two LFIA formats were developed, and their performance was assessed against the reference ELISA using 90 human serum samples. The results showed that the QD-based LFIA achieved a positive percent agreement of 100% and a negative percent agreement of 98.2%, while the GNP-based LFIA had a positive percent agreement of 96.9% and a negative percent agreement of 98.2%. The study concluded that the QD-based LFIA is a feasible method for qualitative antibody detection against the recombinant HAdV-B3 hexon fragment. The findings suggest that such assays could be useful for rapid and accessible serological testing, which has implications for monitoring immunity and vaccine efficacy. However, the study's limited sample size and lack of long-term follow-up data may affect the generalisability of the results, making the evidence strength moderate.

title: Molecular and clinical characterization of human adenovirus in hospitalized pediatric respiratory infections: a five-year study

analysis.research_question_and_background: Human adenovirus (HAdV) is a major pathogen responsible for respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in children in China. This study aimed to characterize the epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and associations with different genotypes and co-detections of HAdV in hospitalized pediatric cases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: This study analyzed clinical data from hospitalized pediatric HAdV infections over a five-year period at Hebei Children’s Hospital between 2016 and 2020. A total of 42,044 children with RTIs were included in the study.
analysis.methods: A retrospective analysis was conducted using sputum samples collected for viral nucleic acid detection and HAdV genotyping, along with demographic, clinical, and laboratory data. Statistical analyses included χ2 tests, Mann–Whitney U tests, and Kruskal–Wallis tests.
analysis.main_results: Among 42,044 samples, 3,123 (7.43%) tested positive for HAdV. Of these, 1,954 (62.6%) had viral co-detection, most commonly with HRV, RSV, and HPIV. The highest HAdV infection rate occurred in children aged 1–3 years (χ2 = 418.44, P = 0.014).
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: HAdV-7 was more frequently detected in patients with severe clinical manifestations, accompanied by decreased immune indices and elevated levels of procalcitonin, D-dimer, as well as cardiac and liver injury markers. HAdV-7 was associated with more severe diseases.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide insights into the epidemiology and clinical impact of HAdV in hospitalized children, particularly highlighting the association of HAdV-7 with severe disease outcomes, which may inform targeted surveillance and management strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is based on retrospective data, which may introduce bias and limit the ability to establish causality. The evidence is moderate in strength due to the observational nature of the study and potential confounding factors.

analysis.summary_en: This study conducted a five-year retrospective analysis of hospitalized pediatric respiratory infections in Hebei Children’s Hospital to characterize human adenovirus (HAdV) epidemiology, clinical manifestations, and associations with genotypes and co-detections. It found that 7.43% of 42,044 samples tested positive for HAdV, with the highest infection rate in children aged 1–3 years. HAdV-7 was more frequently detected in severe cases, associated with decreased immune indices and elevated markers of cardiac and liver injury. The study highlights the clinical significance of HAdV-7 and provides insights for targeted surveillance and management. However, the retrospective design limits the strength of the evidence, and the findings should be interpreted cautiously due to potential biases and confounding factors.

title: [Metagenomic sequencing-based pathogen analysis in pediatric severe acute non-A-E hepatitis].

analysis.research_question_and_background: This study aimed to investigate the role of human adenoviruses in pediatric severe acute non-A-E hepatitis, addressing the need to understand the etiology of such cases and identify potential pathogens.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A case series study was conducted involving 36 children with severe acute non-A-E hepatitis admitted to 17 hospitals between April and July 2022.
analysis.methods: Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) was performed on all 36 patients, and clinical data, including etiological test results and liver function tests, were collected. PCR was used to test for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-DNA and cytomegalovirus (CMV)-DNA in 31 and 25 cases, respectively.
analysis.main_results: Among the 36 children, 24 were male and 12 female, with an onset age of 3.5 (1.1, 9.0) years. No patient tested positive for both human adenovirus and AAV2 simultaneously. Human adenovirus and AAV2 were not detected in any of the patients.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted that the detection rates of human adenovirus and AAV2 are low in children with severe acute non-A-E hepatitis, and there are no co-infection cases with both viruses, highlighting the limited role of these viruses in the condition.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that human adenovirus and AAV2 may not be significant contributors to severe acute non-A-E hepatitis in children, which could inform future diagnostic and surveillance strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its observational design and the lack of control groups, but the evidence is strong due to the comprehensive use of mNGS and PCR methods on a well-characterized cohort.

analysis.summary_en: This study investigated the role of human adenoviruses in pediatric severe acute non-A-E hepatitis through metagenomic sequencing and PCR testing. It enrolled 36 children admitted to 17 hospitals between April and July 2022, analyzing clinical data and specimens. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing (mNGS) detected 11 viruses in plasma samples, but human adenovirus and AAV2 were not found. PCR testing for EBV and CMV also yielded negative results. The authors concluded that human adenovirus and AAV2 have low detection rates and no co-infection cases in this condition. These findings suggest that these viruses may not play a major role in severe acute non-A-E hepatitis in children, potentially guiding future diagnostic approaches. The study's evidence is strong but limited by its observational nature and lack of control groups.

title: Dose-dependent efficacy of intravenous brincidofovir across adenovirus species in immunocompromised patients.

analysis.research_question_and_background: Invasive infections caused by different human adenovirus (HAdV) species represent a life-threatening complication in immunocompromised patients, but no approved antiviral treatment is currently available.
analysis.study_design_and_population: Using PCR-based screening and next-generation sequencing (NGS), we monitored immunocompromised patients with invasive HAdV infection (n=31) enrolled in the phase 2a ATHENA trial, which evaluated optimal dosing regimens of intravenous brincidofovir (BCV).
analysis.methods: Quantitative viral load monitoring indicated sustained clearance of any HAdV species from peripheral blood within five weeks of treatment in the patient cohort treated with the BCV dosing regimen identified as optimal (0.4mg/kg twice weekly).
analysis.main_results: Molecular typing of blood and stool specimens revealed the presence of nearly all HAdV species (A-F), including both common and rarely observed genotypes.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: These findings support a dose-dependent broad efficacy of intravenous BCV across all relevant HAdV species and set the stage for an ensuing phase 3 trial, facilitating future regulatory approval of the compound for this urgently needed indication.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings provide critical evidence for the potential use of intravenous brincidofovir in treating invasive human adenovirus infections in immunocompromised patients, which is a significant unmet medical need.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The supplied evidence does not report limitations, but the study is a phase 2a trial with a relatively small sample size (n=31), which may limit the generalisability of the findings.

analysis.summary_en: This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy of intravenous brincidofovir (BCV) in treating invasive human adenovirus (HAdV) infections in immunocompromised patients. The phase 2a ATHENA trial enrolled 31 patients with HAdV infection, and molecular typing of blood and stool specimens revealed the presence of nearly all HAdV species (A-F), including both common and rarely observed genotypes. Quantitative viral load monitoring showed sustained clearance of any HAdV species from peripheral blood within five weeks of treatment using the optimal dosing regimen of 0.4mg/kg twice weekly. The authors concluded that these findings support a dose-dependent broad efficacy of intravenous BCV across all relevant HAdV species, setting the stage for a phase 3 trial. The study provides important insights into the potential use of BCV for treating HAdV infections in immunocompromised individuals, which is a critical public health need. However, the relatively small sample size may limit the generalisability of the results, and the evidence is considered moderate in strength.

title: Genetic evolution and vaccine challenges in norovirus genogroup II infection

analysis.scope_and_question: Norovirus genogroup II (GII) is the most common etiology of acute gastroenteritis on a global level, and this is due to a significant degree of genetic heterogeneity, rapid adaptive evolution, and extremely efficient person-to-person and environmental transmission systems.
analysis.evidence_base_and_review_method: This review combines current evidence on the evolutionary dynamics of norovirus GII, which defines the patterns of genotype replacement, the recombination mechanisms between ORF1 and ORF2, and the structural factors of antigenic variability that contribute to immune evasion and determine the epidemiology in the world.
analysis.consensus_and_key_conclusions: Genotypes including GII.2, GII.3, and GII.6 remain relatively stable over decades yet continue to account for a substantial proportion of disease. Within GII, rapidly evolving lineages such as GII.4 and episodically emerging genotypes like GII.17 (driven by capsid antigenic drift and novel open reading frame 1/open reading frame 2 (ORF1/ORF2) recombinants) exhibit frequent adaptation and multi-continent expansion.
analysis.controversies_and_evidence_gaps: Key gaps remain in understanding, requiring focused research and policy efforts to improve vaccines and control strategies.
analysis.research_and_practice_implications: We also review advances in diagnostics, including reverse transcription quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), digital PCR, new isothermal amplification, biosensor platforms, and wastewater surveillance, which are collectively sensitive and more accurate in quantification, and in real-time monitoring in the clinical, food safety, and environmental fields.

analysis.summary_en: This review focuses on the genetic evolution and vaccine challenges associated with norovirus genogroup II (GII) infections. It highlights the significant genetic heterogeneity and rapid adaptive evolution of GII, which contribute to its global prevalence as a cause of acute gastroenteritis. The review identifies GII.4 and GII.17 as rapidly evolving and episodically emerging lineages, respectively, driven by antigenic drift and recombination events. While some genotypes like GII.2, GII.3, and GII.6 remain relatively stable, they still account for a substantial proportion of disease. The review also discusses the limitations in vaccine development, including the lack of robust correlates of protection and cross-genotype efficacy. Furthermore, it outlines advances in diagnostic methods and emphasizes the need for targeted research and policy efforts to address gaps in understanding and improve control strategies.
